title: Earth, Sun and Moon
seo_title: Year 7 Science: Earth, Sun and Moon Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Model the cyclic changes in the relative positions of the Earth, sun and moon and explain how these result in phenomena including seasons, phases of the moon, eclipses and tides (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 7 science worksheets on the Earth, Sun and Moon: phases of the Moon, solar and lunar eclipses, tides and seasons, seen from Australia. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Positions in space cause phases, eclipses and tides.
key_sub: The Moon's orbit causes phases and tides; Earth's tilt causes seasons.
body_html:
How to think about it

The movements of the Sun, Earth and Moon cause regular patterns.

  • Phases: half the Moon is always lit; as it orbits Earth we see different amounts of the lit half (about 29.5 days for a full cycle).
  • Eclipses: a solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun (new moon); a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon (full moon).
  • Tides: the Moon's gravity pulls the oceans, giving about two high tides a day. Seasons come from Earth's tilted axis.
Example

What comes after first quarter?

the lit part keeps growing

Answer: waxing gibbous

Example

High tide 6:00 am. Next high tide?

about 12 h 25 min later

Answer: about 6:25 pm

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Earth's shadow causes the phases.
  • Thinking seasons come from Earth's distance from the Sun.
  • Thinking there is an eclipse every month.

faq.q: What causes the phases of the Moon?
faq.a: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun. As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half, from new moon to full moon and back.
Mainly the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans. The Sun's gravity also helps, giving bigger spring tides at new and full moon.

faq.q: Why does the Moon look different from Australia?
faq.a: People in the southern hemisphere see the Moon upside down compared with people in the northern hemisphere, so a waxing crescent is lit on the left.

items.q: Tonight Ethan sees a waning gibbous. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Kai sees a first quarter. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
c: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so the Sun, Earth and Moon rarely line up exactly.
items.e: Usually the Moon passes above or below the line.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the full moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Noah sees a waning gibbous. About which phase will Noah see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Ruby sees a waxing crescent. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: About how many days after a new moon is the next full moon?
items.e: A full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days, so opposite phases are about half that apart.

items.q: About how long does one cycle of Moon phases take?
items.e: About one month.

items.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
c: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon usually do not line up exactly.
The Sun is too far away.
items.e: They need a near-perfect line-up.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Noah sees a waxing gibbous. About which phase will Noah see about two weeks later?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
c: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
items.e: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
items.e: The tilt changes how directly sunlight reaches each place.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the first quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
c: the 23.5° tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
items.e: Tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

items.q: Tonight Kai sees a full moon. Which phase came just before it?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Tonight Priya sees a waxing gibbous. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: First Nations Australians linked the Moon to tides long before modern science. What does this show?
c: The Moon has no effect on tides.
Careful observation of patterns over time is science.
items.e: Many Yolŋu stories describe the Moon and tides.

items.q: Noah reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Harper reads: “The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: What causes day and night?
c: the Earth spinning on its axis once every 24 hours
the Earth orbiting the Sun once a year
the Sun moving around the Earth
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Why is it unsafe to look directly at a solar eclipse without eclipse glasses?
c: Sunlight can damage your eyes even when most of the Sun is covered.
items.e: Use proper eye protection.

items.q: Tom reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: From Australia, which side of a waxing crescent Moon is lit?
items.e: In the southern hemisphere the Moon looks upside down compared with the northern hemisphere.

items.q: About how many days after a full moon is the next new moon?
items.e: A full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days, so opposite phases are about half that apart.

items.q: Noah reads: “Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: William reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” What is this?
items.e: Solar: Moon blocks the Sun. Lunar: Earth's shadow on the Moon.

items.q: Ruby reads: “People in a narrow path on Earth see the Sun's disk completely covered for a few minutes.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: Why should you never look straight at a solar eclipse?
c: The Sun's light can permanently damage your eyes.
items.e: Use eclipse glasses or a pinhole viewer.

items.q: When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, what does the Southern Hemisphere have?
items.e: The seasons are opposite.

items.q: Why do we have seasons?
c: The Sun gets hotter in summer.
The Moon blocks the Sun in winter.
The Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer.
The Earth's axis is tilted, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year.
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the first quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Jack reads: “The Moon turns a reddish colour for over an hour, and everyone on the night side of Earth can see it.” During which Moon phase can this happen?
items.e: Solar eclipses happen only at new moon; lunar eclipses only at full moon.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
c: about 27 days (and about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next)
items.e: This is roughly a month.

items.q: What happens in a solar eclipse?
c: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun.
Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon.
items.e: Solar eclipses happen at new moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the full moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Is the far side of the Moon always dark?
c: No. It gets sunlight too; we just never see it from Earth.
items.e: It is fully lit at new moon.

items.q: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
items.e: The Sun's huge mass pulls them.

items.q: Mia models the Moon's phases with a lamp, a ball and her head. What does the lamp represent?
items.e: Her head is Earth.

items.q: What happens in a lunar eclipse?
c: The Moon disappears for a week.
Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
The Sun passes in front of the Moon.
items.e: Lunar eclipses happen at full moon.

items.q: What mainly causes ocean tides?
c: the pull of the Moon's gravity on Earth's oceans
items.e: The Sun's gravity has a smaller effect.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of the Sun, Earth and Moon?
c: Models are more accurate than observations.
The real distances and sizes are too big to see at once.
items.e: Models help explain patterns.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the last quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Tonight Priya sees a new moon. Which phase comes next?
items.e: The cycle is new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent, about 29.5 days.

items.q: Kai says the phases happen because Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Which observation shows he is wrong?
c: A crescent moon can be seen when the Moon is near the Sun in the sky, where Earth's shadow cannot reach.
items.e: Phases depend on the viewing angle, not Earth's shadow.

items.q: Why are tides about 50 minutes later each day?
c: The Moon moves along its orbit, so Earth must turn a bit further to face it again.
items.e: The Moon's position changes each day.

items.q: Jack records high tide times: Monday 7:10 am, Tuesday 8:00 am, Wednesday 8:50 am. Predict Thursday's morning high tide.
items.e: Each day is about 50 minutes later.

items.q: What is the name of our galaxy?
items.e: A spiral galaxy.

items.q: How many high tides do most Australian beaches have each day?
items.e: High tides happen about every 12 hours 25 minutes.

items.q: When are neap tides (the smallest tides) most likely?
c: at first and last quarter moon
items.e: The Sun and Moon pull at right angles.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the new moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: High tide is at 6:00 am. When is the next high tide, roughly?
items.e: Tides repeat about every 12 hours 25 minutes.

items.q: Which part of Australia has some of the biggest tides, up to about 11 m?
c: the Kimberley coast in Western Australia
items.e: The shape of the coast makes tides bigger there.

items.q: Ella photographs the Moon at 8 pm each night. On which night will it rise latest?
c: the night after the full moon
the night of the new moon
every night at the same time
items.e: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each night.

items.q: When is it summer in Australia?
items.e: Australia is in the southern hemisphere.

items.q: What is the Sun?
items.e: The closest star to Earth.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge group of billions of stars
items.e: We live in the Milky Way.

items.q: Which is bigger: the Solar System or the Moon?
items.e: Moon < Earth < Sun < Solar System < galaxy < Universe.

items.q: It is December. How high is the noon Sun in the sky where Lachlan lives in the Northern Hemisphere, compared with the rest of the year?
c: higher than at any other time of year
lower than at any other time of year
exactly overhead every day of the year
items.e: The tilt towards the Sun makes the noon Sun higher in summer and lower in winter.

items.q: Which is bigger: the Sun or the Earth?
items.e: Moon < Earth < Sun < Solar System < galaxy < Universe.

items.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
c: the force of gravity between them
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Betelgeuse is about 550 light years away. How long does its light take to reach us?
items.e: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, so the light takes 550 years.

items.q: Which star is closer to Earth: Proxima Centauri (4.2 light years) or Sirius (8.6 light years)?
items.e: Fewer light years means closer.

items.q: It is September. Kai lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: Vega is about 25 light years away. How long does its light take to reach us?
items.e: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, so the light takes 25 years.

items.q: Why does the Moon shine?
c: It reflects light from the Sun.
It reflects light from the Earth only.
items.e: The Moon is not a light source.

items.q: Is the Sun the biggest star in the Universe?
c: No. Many stars are much bigger than the Sun.
items.e: The Sun is a medium-sized star.

items.q: It is March. Noah lives in the Northern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: At about what angle is the Earth's axis tilted?
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: Which is smaller: the Universe or the Solar System?
items.e: Moon < Earth < Sun < Solar System < galaxy < Universe.

items.q: It is June. How high is the noon Sun in the sky where Zara lives in the Northern Hemisphere, compared with the rest of the year?
c: higher than at any other time of year
lower than at any other time of year
exactly overhead every day of the year
items.e: The tilt towards the Sun makes the noon Sun higher in summer and lower in winter.

items.q: Which is smaller: the Earth or the Moon?
items.e: Moon < Earth < Sun < Solar System < galaxy < Universe.

items.q: It is December. Priya lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: Why do stars look tiny?
c: They are smaller than the Moon.
items.e: Distance.

items.q: Why is it warmer in summer?
c: The Earth is much closer to the Sun.
The Sun is higher in the sky, so its energy is more concentrated and the days are longer.
items.e: The tilt of the Earth causes the seasons; its spin causes day and night.

items.q: It is June. William lives in the Southern Hemisphere. Which season is it there?
items.e: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun has summer; the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.

items.q: What is a light year?
c: the distance light travels in one year
the time it takes light to travel one year
a year on a light planet
items.e: A unit of distance.

items.q: Why does the Moon have phases?
c: Earth's shadow covers part of it.
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.
items.e: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

items.q: Liam sees a first-quarter Moon. What fraction of the Moon's face looks lit?
items.e: "Quarter" means a quarter of the way through the cycle.

items.q: Which model best explains a solar eclipse?
c: Sun → Moon → Earth in a straight line
Earth → Sun → Moon in a straight line
Sun → Earth → Moon in a straight line
items.e: The Moon's shadow hits Earth.

items.q: When we look at a star 100 light years away, what are we seeing?
c: the star as it is right now
light that left the star 100 years ago
items.e: Looking back in time.

items.q: Ruby draws the Moon every night for a month. What pattern will she see?
c: The Moon is the same every night.
The lit part grows to full, then shrinks back to new.
items.e: The cycle repeats about every 29.5 days.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Mei models phases with a lamp (Sun), a ball (Moon) and her head (Earth). Where should the ball be to show a full moon?
c: between her head and the lamp
on the opposite side of her head from the lamp
items.e: Full moon: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.

items.q: Why do surf lifesavers record tide times on beach boards?
c: Tides change water depth and currents, which affects swimmers' safety.
items.e: Knowing the tide keeps beachgoers safe.

items.q: Why would you weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
c: The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass.
The Moon is closer to the Sun.
There is no gravity on the Moon.
Your mass is less on the Moon.
items.e: Weight depends on gravity.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Why do astronomers use light years and not kilometres?
c: It is a rule from the Moon.
The distances are so huge that kilometres give enormous numbers.
Kilometres do not work in space.
items.e: Convenient units.

items.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
c: The Moon rotates once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth.
items.e: Synchronous rotation.

items.q: In Mia's model, when does the ball look fully lit?
c: when the ball is between her and the lamp
when the ball is on the opposite side of her head from the lamp
items.e: That is a full moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the new moon?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waxing crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: Noah sees a lunar eclipse from Perth. Who else on Earth could see it at the same time?
c: everyone on the night side of Earth
items.e: Earth's shadow is on the Moon itself.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes after the waning crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.

items.q: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, what would happen?
c: Summer would last all year everywhere.
There would be no day and night.
There would be almost no seasons.
items.e: Tilt causes seasons.

items.q: Why do more people see a lunar eclipse than a total solar eclipse?
c: Everyone on Earth's night side can see the shadowed Moon, but the Moon's shadow on Earth is small.
Lunar eclipses last only a second.
items.e: Earth's shadow is large.
